passages.text: The sorting line has a monocular camera inside its colour hood, 40 mm before the colour sensor. Its mount, lens and trigger are proven against the model in stf-cad/hbw/vision/mount.py. In the 3D twin, the camera photographs every baked cookie at the moment the cookie passes under the lens: 1. The scene is rendered off screen from the camera's own pose and lens (web/src/vision/photo.ts). The photo is 256 × 256 px, looks straight down at the belt, and is lit by the ring light's flash. 2. The photo is posted to the API, which validates it and stores it (services/api/captures.py). 3. The dashboard's Vision QC page shows the newest photos under Photos from the camera.

Route | What it does: Route POST /vision/captures?flavour=chocolate&n=3&source=twin, What it does Stores one photo. The body is the JPEG (Content-Type: image/jpeg).; Route GET /vision/captures?limit=48, What it does Returns the guest's newest photos' records: id, t, flavour, n, source, bytes, w, h.; Route GET /vision/captures/{id}.jpg, What it does Returns one of the guest's photos.

Each photo belongs to the guest whose twin took it (DATABASE.md): a visitor sees and opens only their own. A table made before guests existed needs the column: alter table public.captures add column owner text not null default ''; create index capturesowner on public.captures (owner, t desc); Uploads come from visitors' browsers, so every upload is checked: - the request comes from the app's own origin; - the body is a real JPEG between 32 and 1024 px and at most 200 kB; - the flavour is a known one; - a client may send at most a burst of 4 photos, then one every 3 s; - the server accepts at most STFCAPTUREDAILY photos a day (default 500).

Many people use the deployed site at once, and none of them should see another's data. Until sign-in (SSO) arrives, every visitor is a guest. The server issues the guest the first time the browser reaches the API, and the browser keeps it in a cookie.

services/api/guests.py: - Issued by the server, not claimed by the browser. A random 128-bit id in the cookie stfguest = <id.<signature. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256 with STFSESSIONSECRET, so an id cannot be forged or guessed into someone else's. Whatever X-STF-User header a browser sends is replaced by the guest's id. - A safe cookie. HttpOnly (page scripts cannot read it), SameSite=Lax (other sites' requests do not carry it), Secure over HTTPS, Path=/, kept for STFGUESTDAYS (default 30). - No personal data. A guest record is its id, when it was made, when it was last seen and how many visits. No IP address, no browser fingerprint. - Visible in the twin. The top bar shows the session id and which database holds its data (web/src/twin/TopBar.tsx); the Orders panel's Session history section reads GET /twin/records back: the order lines this

visitor's twin finished and the cookies its camera judged, newest first (web/src/shared/session.ts, web/src/shared/records.ts). Two visitors on the deployed site are two guests: neither sees the other's rows. - Lapses on its own. A guest unseen for STFGUESTDAYS is removed with its conversations. - Forget me. DELETE /guest removes the guest's conversations, photos and live twin at once, and clears the cookie. GET /guest shows the guest's record and which database is in use. - A crawler cannot fill the table. A client may start 20 guests, then one a minute.

QC testing. In every 12 cookies one is damaged on purpose (burnt, underbaked or cracked), in the twin and in the month alike: the camera rejects it and the cell bakes it again. So every order in orders has a qcfault, bakes one cookie more than it delivers, and the month's quality is 90 %. Loading it. make db-seed removes the rows it loaded last time (the guests' own twin orders and inspections stay) and loads the factory tables again from the files the dashboard reads, then stores the ten sample photos (their records in captures, the JPEGs in the bucket) with their decisions in inspections. make db-seed RESET=1 first forgets every guest, conversation and photo. Run it again whenever the simulations change, and the database matches the dashboard again. The twin. POST /twin/inspection (each judged cookie) and POST /twin/order
(each finished order line) store the guest's own rows; GET /twin/records returns them. The twin sends them as it runs (web/src/shared/records.ts); the public demo, with no API, sends nothing.

A signed-in user replaces the guest as the owner. guests.current() is the one place the API asks who the visitor is, and every store keys its documents by that owner. Migrating a guest's data to the user it signs in as is one update of owner in each table.
Two things can be deployed. Both are free.

| What it is | Needs a server? | Free host | Sleeps?: The public demo (stf-twin), What it is The standalone twin. The 3D cell, the orders, the compiled PLC program, the vision CNN, the AAS and OPC UA browsers all run in the visitor's browser., Needs a server? No: static files (web/dist-pages), Free host Render Static Site, GitHub Pages, Firebase, Sleeps? Never; The live twin (stf-live), What it is The Python physics kernel (services/api) streaming the machine over a WebSocket, with the web app served by the same process., Needs a server? Yes: one container (Dockerfile), Free host Google Cloud Run (see GCPDEPLOY.md), Render, Sleeps? Scales to 0 / wakes in seconds

For a portfolio link, use the public demo: it is always on and costs nothing at any traffic level. The live twin can be hosted for free on Google Cloud Run or Render to demonstrate live server-side kinematics and WebSockets.

The repository is the whole project; everything the builds need is committed (the generated data in web/public included). Heavy and local-only files (.venv, nodemodules, .cache, FreeCAD backups) are ignored.

Render adds the other headers from render.yaml (X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy). - The live twin is read-only to the public. A command is accepted only with the operator token: Render generates STFAPITOKEN (dashboard → stf-live → Environment), sent as the X-STF-Token header. Its own https://…onrender.com origin is allowed automatically (RENDEREXTERNALURL); the API sends the same security headers as vite preview (services/api/app.py). See docs/SECURITY.md. - WebSocket clients are capped (STFMAXWSCLIENTS, 16 on Render) and commands are rate-limited. - Every visitor is a guest of their own (a signed, HttpOnly cookie): their copilot conversations, inspection photos and live twin are theirs alone. Render generates STFSESSIONSECRET; guests and their chats are kept in SQLite until the next deploy, or in Supabase across deploys. See DATABASE.md.

The dashboard's Ask button and the Copilot page answer with Gemini when the API service has a key, and offline otherwise (always on the static demo). The key lives only on the server: - Locally: put GEMINIAPIKEY=... in .env at the repo root (git-ignored; see .env.example) and restart the API. - Render: dashboard → stf-live → Environment → set GEMINIAPIKEY (the Blueprint declares it without a value). The model calls the twin's tools (services/api/tools.py) and may state only what they return; the server checks every number in the answer (verify.py) and cites the sources. Each client is rate-limited and the daily caps protect the quota. When a model reaches its limit, the next one answers. Each Gemini model has its own quota, so the server keeps an ordered list and takes a model out for as long as Google's error

says (retryDelay), then tries the next; when every Gemini model is out, a local model (Ollama) answers if one runs, and otherwise the twin's tools answer directly. GET /chat/status shows which models are free. Conversations are kept as JSON documents, one per session (services/api/store.py, under STFDATADIR, default .data/), owned by an anonymous id the browser keeps. Each session carries a context store - the facts the tools established - that whichever model answers next is given, so a hand-over from Gemini to the local model keeps the thread. The store has the shape of a NoSQL one (get / put / delete / list by owner), so MongoDB or Firestore can replace it. On Render's free tier the disk is ephemeral: history lasts until the next deploy. Spoken answers (🔊 on each answer, and the Voice tab) go through one

speech pipeline, POST /chat/tts - see docs/TTSPIPELINE.md to use it from another site: ElevenLabs when ELEVENLABSAPIKEY is set, then Gemini TTS (2.5 Pro first, the flash voices while its quota is closed - on the free tier the Pro voice has none), then the computer's own voice (macOS say). Ollama serves language models, not speech. The Voice tab hears questions with the browser's speech recognition, or records them for POST /chat/stt (Gemini transcription) where the browser has none.

The entire digital twin (interactive 3D Three.js frontend + FastAPI physics kernel + WebSocket at 30 Hz + Grounded Industrial Copilot) is containerized in Dockerfile and runs natively on Google Cloud Run.

$0 Free Tier: Cloud Run provides 2 million requests/month, 360,000 GiB-seconds of memory, and 180,000 vCPU-seconds per month for free. Native WebSockets: Full bi-directional streaming for /ws live 30 Hz machine frames. Automatic HTTPS: Provides a managed, public SSL URL (e.g. https://stf-live-xxxxxx-ew.a.run.app). Scale to Zero: Shuts down when idle to preserve resources, and cold-starts in 1–2 seconds. Cloud Build: Google Cloud builds the container image remotely — you do not even need Docker installed locally.

passages.text: The full kit chains four modules (only the first two are simulated so far): 1. Automated High-Bay Warehouse (Automatisiertes Hochregallager, HRL/HBW) 2. Vacuum Gripper Robot (Vakuum-Sauggreifer, VSG/VGR) 3. Multi-processing station with kiln/oven (Multi-Bearbeitungsstation mit Brennofen) 4. Sorting line with colour detection (Sortierstrecke mit Farkerkennung) Material flow (manual §"Verkettung"): the vacuum gripper loads workpieces onto the stacker crane of the high-bay warehouse, which stores them sorted by colour; for retrieval the crane returns carriers to the conveyor and the gripper picks the workpiece back off.

Scope: the live API (services/api), the web app and how it is served (web/), the infrastructure (docker-compose.yml, mosquitto/), the Python model and analytics code (stf-cad/hbw), and the dependencies of all of them. The machine-side security design (IEC 62443 zones, the Modbus allow-list, the hardwired interlocks) is Upgrades 11 and 12, documented in UPGRADEPLAN.md. This document covers the software that runs the twin.

| Finding | Severity | Status: S1, Finding POST /command had no authentication. It was reachable through the public ngrok link, so anyone with the link could command the machine., Severity High, Status Fixed. Commands are accepted from the operator's own machine (Host is localhost) or with the operator token STFAPITOKEN (X-STF-Token header). A tunnel is read-only.; S2, Finding CORS alloworigins=[""]: any website open in the operator's browser could call the API on localhost (CSRF)., Severity High, Status Fixed. An origin allow-list (STFALLOWEDORIGINS), and a foreign Origin is refused for commands even towards localhost.; S3, Finding The Vite proxy rewrote Host to 127.0.0.1:8000 (changeOrigin), which made every tunnelled request look local and bypassed S1. Found while verifying S1., Severity High, Status Fixed. changeOrigin: false and xfwd: true. A comment in vite.config.ts says why it must stay that way.

| Finding | Severity | Status: S4, Finding The WebSocket had no origin check (cross-site WebSocket hijacking), no client cap and no message size limit., Severity Medium, Status Fixed. Origin check, 32 clients (STFMAXWSCLIENTS), 1 KB messages, and only {"type": "resync"} is understood.; S5, Finding Infrastructure published on every interface: Redis with no password, Postgres with password stf, MQTT anonymous., Severity High (when run), Status Fixed. Ports bound to 127.0.0.1. Redis and Postgres passwords are required from .env (see .env.example; .env is git-ignored). Mosquitto refuses anonymous clients and uses a password file.; S6, Finding The public link served the Vite dev server: source maps, module graph, HMR socket., Severity Medium, Status Fixed. The tunnel now serves the production build (vite preview, port 4173) with security headers. The dev server listens on localhost only.

| Finding | Severity | Status: S7, Finding No security headers., Severity Medium, Status Fixed. A strict CSP: scripts from self only (plus wasm-unsafe-eval for the mesh decoder, never unsafe-eval). Also frame-ancestors 'none', nosniff, no-referrer, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy and COOP. The theme pre-paint script moved out of the HTML so no inline script is needed.; S8, Finding Commands validated deep in the runtime only (op a free string, slot unchecked at the boundary)., Severity Low, Status Fixed. op is one of a fixed set of four, and slot must match ^[A-C][1-4]$. Anything else gets a 422. Commands are rate-limited per client (token bucket, 4/s, burst 8).; S9, Finding torch.load of pickled checkpoints: code execution if a .pt file is replaced., Severity Medium, Status Fixed. weightsonly=True in ml/tune.py and validate.py.

One endpoint on 127.0.0.1, Basic256Sha256 Sign & Encrypt only; user name and password from STFOPCUAUSER / STFOPCUAPASSWORD (12 characters or more), compared in constant time; no anonymous token; client certificates must be in the trust list; every variable read-only. opcua/check.py proves each refusal against a running server, and a mutant that allows anonymous access is caught.

Mosquitto's existing configuration listened in plain text, and an MQTT broker gives every client every topic unless told otherwise., Severity High (when run), Status Designed out. One listener on 127.0.0.1, TLS 1.3 only, with the cell's own CA; no anonymous clients; one account per role (edge, host, viewer, auditor) with random passwords kept readable by the user only; an access list per role, so the edge writes only its own Sparkplug topics, only the host sends commands and writes the UNS, and the viewer only reads the UNS. uns/check.py proves four refused connections, six forbidden writes never delivered and a forbidden read; mutants that allow anonymous access or let the edge command itself are caught.
Python dependencies: pip-audit finds no known vulnerabilities. npm: 0 in production dependencies, and only S12 remains in development.

- tests/testapisecurity.py covers the cases below, and the full suite (100 tests) passes: - local commands are accepted; - commands through a tunnel are refused, but accepted with the token and refused with a wrong one; - a CSRF attempt from a foreign origin is refused; - a DNS-rebinding host name is refused; - malformed operations and slots are rejected; - the rate limiter works; - a WebSocket from a foreign origin is closed, and one from the app's own origin streams. - Against the running system through the public link: - a command gets a 403, and reads get a 200; - the CSP and the other headers are present; - /stf/src/... returns the app shell, not source; - the 3D view (including the WebAssembly decoder) and the live stream work under the CSP.

- To command the machine from another device, set STFAPITOKEN and send it as X-STF-Token. Never put the token in a URL. - Share the production build only: npm run build && npm run preview on port 4173, and tunnel that port.

A spoken question goes through three steps, and each step has its own job: ElevenLabs only listens and speaks. It turns the operator's recording into text and reads an answer aloud. It never writes an answer: every answer comes from the copilot's language models (Groq first), from the twin's tools and documents. Only services/api/tts.py calls ElevenLabs, and tests/testvoice.py checks that no other module does and that ElevenLabs is never one of the chat's models. Measured on 2026-10-18 (make voice-check, then the three endpoints in turn):

Step | Provider | Time | Result: Step speech to text, Provider ElevenLabs scribev1, Time 0.7-0.9 s, Result 103-character sentence, every word right; Step speech to text (comparison), Provider Groq whisper-large-v3-turbo, Time 0.3-0.4 s, Result every word right; Step text to answer, Provider Groq openai/gpt-oss-120b, Time 1.0 s, Result route: documents; Step answer to speech, Provider ElevenLabs elevenmultilingualv2, voice 01, Time 1.5 s for 103 characters, 7 s for a long answer (first request after a pause: up to 14 s), Result MP3
elevenflashv25 was not faster here, and its audio was transcribed less exactly ("HPW" for "HBW"), so the multilingual model stays the default.

The answer is {"text": ..., "model": "elevenlabs scribev1"}. Providers are tried in the order STTPROVIDERS (default elevenlabs,groq,gemini); one without a key, at its limit or failing is passed over. GET /chat/stt/status lists them in order, with which are ready. When one is ready, the copilot's Voice tab records the question and the server transcribes it; only without one does it use the browser's own speech recognition.

Provider | Needs | Notes: Provider ElevenLabs Scribe, Needs ELEVENLABSAPIKEY (optional ELEVENLABSSTTMODEL, default scribev1), Notes On HTTP 401 / 402 it is passed over for an hour, on 429 / 503 for a minute.; Provider Groq Whisper, Needs GROQAPIKEY (optional GROQSTTMODEL), Notes The fastest.; Provider Gemini, Needs GEMINIAPIKEY (GEMINISTTMODELS in turn), Notes Free-tier daily quota.

One HTTP endpoint turns text into speech, trying providers in order until one speaks. The twin's copilot uses it; any other site (a portfolio, a demo page) can use it the same way. The answer is the audio itself (audio/mpeg from ElevenLabs, audio/wav from Gemini and the local voice), with two headers saying who spoke:
Header | Example: Header X-TTS-Provider, Example elevenlabs, gemini, local; Header X-TTS-Model, Example elevenlabs elevenmultilingualv2, gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts, macOS say
GET /chat/tts/status lists the providers and whether each is ready, and the Gemini voices' quota.

Provider | Needs | Notes: Provider ElevenLabs, Needs ELEVENLABSAPIKEY, the voices ELEVENLABSVOICEID01, ELEVENLABSVOICEID02, ... (ELEVENLABSVOICE picks one, default 01), optional ELEVENLABSMODEL, Notes MP3. On HTTP 401 / 402 it is passed over for an hour, on 429 / 503 for a minute. X-TTS-Model names the voice, e.g. elevenlabs elevenmultilingualv2 voice 01.; Provider Groq, Needs GROQAPIKEY (optional GROQTTSMODEL), Notes WAV.; Provider Gemini, Needs GEMINIAPIKEY, Notes GEMINITTSMODELS in turn: 2.5 Pro TTS (no free-tier quota), 2.5 Flash TTS, 3.8 Flash TTS. Each at its limit is passed over for Google's retry delay.; Provider Local, Needs macOS (say, afconvert), Notes Offline and free. On Linux, replace LocalVoice with Piper or espeak.

Set the order with TTSPROVIDERS, e.g. TTSPROVIDERS=elevenlabs,gemini on a server without the local voice. With none ready the endpoint answers 503 and a browser can fall back to its own speechSynthesis, as the copilot does.
Markdown and [citations] are removed and units are spoken as words ("176 degrees Celsius", "6.16 euros", "O E E"); at most 1 200 characters are spoken, cut at a sentence.

The other site's origin must be in STFALLOWEDORIGINS on the API (requests from other origins are refused), and each client is rate-limited (3 at once, then one every 10 s) under a daily budget (GEMINITTSDAILYLIMIT) - the keys stay on the server. Mathematics and code in an answer are read as "(formula)" and "(code)".

make voice-check uses the real providers and prints no key: 1. which speech-to-text and text-to-speech providers are ready, in order; 2. passages.text: Why. The model already holds what an asset's digital identity needs: part data, documents, 3D files, the bill of material, energy and the AI models. The Asset Administration Shell (IEC 63278) is the standard container for it, and the one the EU's Digital Product Passport and data spaces such as Catena-X build on. Step 2 is OPC UA (IEC 62541), the running machine's information model and a server for it. Step 3 is MQTT Sparkplug B and a Unified Namespace: the event-driven, publish-subscribe side, where every system (SCADA, MES, dashboards, AI agents) reads one shared, current picture of the plant instead of polling each machine.

passages.text: The first run caught the edge ending its session 3.2 s late when the host went offline. It handled the STATE on the MQTT network thread and then waited there for the NDEATH's acknowledgement, which that same thread had to send. - It also caught the host re-announcing itself online in reply to its own clean-shutdown STATE, so the edge was born to a host that was gone. Both are fixed. Limits. - One broker on localhost, MQTT 3.1.1 for the edge and the host. - No Sparkplug templates, historical data or store-and-forward. - The UNS carries the cell's data only. passages.text: Found. - The rollout scheduler is faster in 20 of 25 runs on identical timings (4.4 s per order on average, best 16.2 s, worst 10.8 s slower). The gain is the crane: 198.3 s busy under the PLC, 190.4 s with the moulds stored in the slots that finish the order soonest. Without slot choice the agent found nothing: the program's job priority is already at the rollout optimum. - Q-learning on top does not improve the rollout prior: job times vary and the state does not see time. - Shielded: no deadlock in 1000 training orders and every test. The same agent without the shield deadlocked in 293 of 333 training orders. Limits. Simulated job times; one order of 12 cookies; the shield is exact for this model, not for a plant whose timing leaves the model.

passages.text: Question. Can an operator ask about the cell in plain words and get an answer that is true, sourced and free to run - without a language model? As built: web/src/copilot/copilot.ts, the "Copilot" dashboard page, make copilot. - Tools. A question is routed to a tool that computes the answer from the twin's data: what to service next, a part's remaining life at a machine age, an alarm code, why the line stopped, OEE, energy, carbon, the scheduler, the inspection, the maintenance network, the attacks. Each answer links to the page with the detail. - Documents. Otherwise the best passage of the project's documents (197 passages, BM25), shown with its section. - No guessing. A passage counts only if it covers more than half of the question's words; below that, and with no tool, the answer is "I don't know".

Upgrade 19: the bake as a process (BUILT)
passages.text: Question. The oven waited a fixed time and every cookie came out right. What happens when the bake is heat and water, as in a real oven, and what should the PLC and the hardware do about it? As built: stf-cad/hbw/bake.py (make bake), the "Oven process" dashboard page, the chapter docs/process/README.md (generated) and the copilot's ovenprocess tool. - The oven from its own parts (ovenmodel.py): three thermal nodes (the grill element, the bottom elements, the liner and walls), the tray, and the air as a balance. Elements radiate and convect, the walls lose through the ceramic fibre, and the shut door, the steam vent and the open mouth (buoyant exchange) lose to the hall. A PI controller on the thermocouple drives Q9; the fan stops and the integral holds while the door is open. - The cookie in 16 layers:

path: STF upgrade plan: from training model to industrial practice
Upgrade 19: the bake as a process (BUILT)
passages.text: conduction, radiation from the grill and the liner, contact with the tray. Each layer dries at a rate following water's vapour pressure and takes its latent heat; this is solved implicitly, so the evaporation cools the layer and slows itself. The surface browns with Arrhenius kinetics once dry. Done means 95 C at the centre and at most 6 % water; colour 0.35-0.65. - The order's real door openings (control.py's step table), and the disturbances of a shift: the hall's daily temperature, aged elements, the robot's waits, and dough lots from the bench or the fridge. - Four ways to end a bake, on the same 20 shifts (960 cookies each): a fixed timer; a soft sensor (the PLC runs its own model of the oven and the cookie, corrected by the thermocouple, and learns the elements' ageing); + the

passages.text: Found. - The oven is the bottleneck. With a real bake the cell makes 5.5 cookies an hour; the rest of the cell could feed 14 such ovens. Capacity now means baking many cookies at once (a tunnel oven: STF-2), not a faster crane. - A timer is wrong one cookie in five. Most of those are dough from the fridge. A model of the cookie fixes half of that; the camera most of the rest. Two cheap sensors reading the dough before it goes in make it right 99 times in 100: the hardware this upgrade asks for. - The energy figures change. About 51 Wh of heat per cookie and 266 W to hold 180 C: some 138 kWh a month on two shifts, three times the rest of the cell. The Upgrade 9 microgrid was sized for

passages.text: the 5 W lamp; its 600 W inverter cannot run 1 300 W of elements, so Upgrade 9 and Upgrade 18 need re-running with the oven. - Door openings overshoot. After each one the air reaches at most 199 C, 51 K below the cutout. Proofs. The energy ledger closes on every shift (to machine precision). The heat-up (296 s) matches ovenmodel.py's ~6 min, the elements peak at 731 C (sheath 800 C), and the hold power lies within its loss bounds. 16 layers at 0.5 s agree with 32 at 0.1 s within 2 %, and an unstable step is refused before it runs. Thicker or colder dough bakes longer, a hotter oven shorter, and weaker elements heat up more slowly. The wet centre holds near 100 C. Each policy is at least as good as the one before,

passages.text: and the best reaches 97 %. Four mutations are each caught: the steam off the ledger, an 8 s step, browning that slows with heat, and doors that lose no heat. Limits. Every material value and disturbance is assumed; the drying and browning rates are calibrated so a nominal 8 mm cookie reaches its colour in about 10 min at 180 C. One measured bake (a thermocouple in a dough piece, a colour reading) replaces the calibration. The cookie is one-dimensional (no edge browning), and it does not rise or spread.

One production cell exists twice: as a physical fischertechnik training factory on a desk, and as an interactive 3D twin in the browser. Both are built from the same machine model, so a number read on the dashboard traces back to the same mechanism it names. This page pairs the two, module by module.

path: Two views of the same machine
passages.text: The renders below are the design ground truth of the physical cell — what the machine on the desk is laid out to be. The screenshots are the digital setup: the live web twin running the same mechanisms, the same PLC program and the same timing model. Figure: The whole production cell as designed: warehouse on the left, vacuum gripper robot and oven in the middle, sorting line on the right. Figure: The same cell running in the web twin, mid-order: the stacker crane serving the rack, the vacuum robot over the oven, the sorting line hood to the right.

The 3 × 4 rack of moulds and the stacker crane that serves it. In the twin, pick any bay from the order form or the view switcher and watch the crane's rack-and-pinion drive count each rack position. Figure: The high-bay warehouse: the rack of moulds, the stacker crane and its belt.

The gantry arm that carries a mould and its cup of dough between the warehouse belt, the oven and the sorting line — the busiest mechanism in the cell. Figure: The vacuum gripper robot between the warehouse belt, the oven and the sorting line. Figure: Inside the cell in the twin: the robot's X/Y gantry over the oven, with the Ofenschieber and the Drehtisch visible.

The chamber with the Drehtisch (rotary table), the saw for dividing the dough, and the Ofenschieber (pusher) that slides the mould in and out. The 2 s lamp bake is the physical demo; the full baking time model lives in the twin. Figure: The oven: the chamber with its controller display, the Drehtisch with the saw, and the belt to the sorting line.

The belt, the colour hood with the inspection camera 40 mm before the colour sensor, three ejectors and their Lagerstellen. Figure: The sorting line: the belt, the colour hood with the inspection camera, three ejectors and their Lagerstellen.

The controller the whole cell obeys. The twin runs the same program, generated from the same export the reference documents are drawn from — so the I/O names and unit sequencers you read in the docs are the ones the twin executes. Figure: The PLC cabinet with its controller and wiring.

path: Where the twin differs on purpose
passages.text: - Speed. The physical demo bakes in about 2 s under a lamp so a class can watch a full order in minutes. The twin models the full bake and transfer times, and the fast-forward control (1× / 2× / 4× / 8×) lets you watch either horizon. - Faults. Alarms, watchdogs and safety reactions are commissioned by injecting faults into the twin — things you would not do to the desk machine. - Scale. Every number on the dashboard is computed from the twin's model (the same up12 export), not typed in: production, health, maintenance, energy and alarms all trace to one source.

The control cabinet holds one controller and the safety circuit; each module has its own remote I/O node on its plate, reached over Ethernet (Modbus TCP). The modules keep their fischertechnik 24 V sensors and actuators, wired to the node through the adaptor PCB. Figure: The control cabinet in the 3D twin: the controller, the 24 V supply, the safety relay and contactors on the DIN rail.

PROGRAM MAIN (lines 1167-1923) is the orchestrator: every scan it reads the units' state, and when a unit finishes a job it offers jobs again in one fixed priority order. A job is bound to its arguments (a cookie, a mould, a slot, a bay) and may need several units at once.

- ESTOP: the two-channel safety relay K0 drops Enable for every unit at once. Every state has a transition to ESTOP on NOT Enable; outputs are off in ESTOP. Leaving it needs the reset S3 through the safety relay, then the unit homes again (ESTOP - INIT). - FAULT: a watchdog or a failed sensor puts one unit in FAULT with its alarm. Outputs are off; the operator clears the cause and acknowledges on the HMI (FAULT - READY on Ack AND Enable). - Force-guided contactors K1 and K2 switch the actuators' 24 V, so a stop removes the power that moves anything, not only the program's command. - Outputs are off in INIT, READY, FAULT and ESTOP (proved, chapter 7).

1. Every unit state reaches READY and ESTOP; outputs are off in INIT, READY, FAULT and ESTOP; no motor is driven both ways; every signal is in the Belegungsplan; every motion has a timeout. 2. The orchestrator, explored exhaustively over every completion order (every possible timing), never deadlocks, conserves 12 cookies and 12 moulds, and ends with every cookie in its bin. 3. Every cookie's trace record is complete, and its flavour is confirmed by the colour sensor. Sources: stf-cad/hbw/control.py (module docstring: PROOFS).

The Smart Tabletop Factory is run by one IEC 61131-3 program: eight unit sequencers and an orchestrator, generated from the same models that prove the machine's motion. The twin compiles it with MatIEC to WebAssembly and runs it in the browser against the simulated plant every 5 ms (software in the loop). Nothing in the 3D view moves unless this program drives an output. Figure: The PLC panel in the 3D twin: the program running, its units' states and its I/O image, live.

- Units: one FUNCTIONBLOCK per unit. Each is a step sequence INIT - homing - READY - job steps - READY, with FAULT and ESTOP reachable from every state. A unit drives only its own outputs. - Orchestrator (PROGRAM MAIN): a PLC scan that, after every job completion, offers the units jobs in one fixed priority order, following the dispatch policy (here: reuse). It tracks the factory state: slots, moulds, belt ends, oven, bins. - Positioning: each axis is driven toward its own target and stops half a scan's travel before it (the brake lead), so a three-axis robot move ends with every axis in tolerance. - Watchdogs: every step that moves something has a time limit (1.5 x nominal + 0.5 s); past it the unit drops its outputs and goes to FAULT with an alarm.

path: Vision QC: the inspection camera and its models
passages.text: A camera in the sorting line's colour hood photographs every cookie. A convolutional network decides whether it is good, an autoencoder checks that it looks like the cookies the network was trained on, and the sorting line acts on the decision: a cookie that does not pass is not ejected to its Lagerstelle but held at the end of the line, and the order makes it again. The camera sees, the network decides, the machine does what it decided: physical AI on a small scale. Figure: A cracked cookie the inspection rejected, held at the end of the sorting line while the order makes it again.

passages.doc: Vision QC: the inspection camera and its models
path: Vision QC: the inspection camera and its models
passages.text: 1. Trigger. The cookie crosses the lens's axis on the sorting belt; the cell takes one photo (web/src/scene/engine/CellCoordinator.ts, camera(): a change of side between two ticks, so fast playback cannot step over it). 2. Photo. The twin renders the camera's view off screen and, at the same instant, the empty hood: the reference image (web/src/vision/photo.ts, expose()). 3. Preparation. The cookie is found against the reference image; everything that is not cookie is set to the belt's own colour; the grey reference target is kept (web/src/vision/twinCamera.ts, prepare()). 4. Decision. The CNN gives the condition, the autoencoder the anomaly score (web/src/vision/inspect.ts, judge()), in the browser, in a few milliseconds. 5. Action. The verdict reaches the cell before the cookie reaches the first ejector (about 4 s of belt at 60 mm/s). On pass it is ejected to its Lagerstelle as before; on

passages.text: reject (or to a person, when the network is unsure) no ejector fires, the belt carries it to the end of the line, the robot finds its bay empty, its mould goes home empty, and the order starts that cookie again from the next raw dough (CellCoordinator.ts, complete(); OvenFlow.ts, buildFlow(..., reject)). The two journeys are the same, at the same speed, up to the ejectors, so the cell can switch a cookie to the reject path the moment the verdict comes in. The reject path needs no hardware the CAD model does not have: the belt simply runs on to its end.

passages.text: In the 3D twin, open Orders and place an order. QC testing is on by default: in every 12 cookies one, drawn at random, is burnt, underbaked or cracked, so every rack tests the inspection. Under Quality inspection you can also choose a fault for the next cookie yourself. Watch the damaged cookie pass the camera, skip its ejector and stop at the end of the line. The card lists each decision: what the cookie really was, what the CNN saw and how sure it was, the autoencoder's score, and whether the call was right, a catch, an escape or a false reject. passages.text: A convolutional autoencoder (26,363 parameters, an 8 x 8 x 8 bottleneck) trained on good cookies only: it never saw a defect and needs no labels. A cookie's anomaly score is the worst 6 x 6 px patch of its reconstruction error; the threshold is the 99th percentile of good cookies. The drift signal is the mean error of good-looking cookies against its training baseline: above twice the baseline, the line no longer looks like training, the cue to collect images and retrain. Source: web/public/vision/autoencoder.json, stf-cad/hbw/vision/autoencoder.py.

passages.text: The 3D cookie carries its fault as its dome's texture, drawn to render.py's definitions: burnt - colour times 0.45, the rim darkened from 60-75 % of the radius out; underbaked - only 30 % of the bake's colour; cracked - a wavy dark line across the top, 1-2 px wide in the camera's image and 60-95 % of the radius long. How the twin decides when a part needs service: what is measured, how wear is modelled, how the noise is smoothed, how the health index and the remaining life are computed, when the two warnings fire, how preventive service changes a part's state, and how the service schedule and the spare parts follow from it. Every equation below is the one the code computes, with the line it is on; every number comes from the health model the dashboard reads. Everything is simulated: the wear laws and lives are assumptions, flagged as such in the model.

Symbol | Meaning | Value: Symbol $n$, Meaning uses of the part (cycles) since it was new, Value ; Symbol $m$, Meaning uses per shift: uses per order x orders per shift, Value orders per shift: 67.0; Symbol $L$, Meaning the part's life in uses (assumed), Value per part, table below; Symbol $p$, Meaning the wear law's exponent, Value per part; Symbol $r_f$, Meaning the signal at which the part fails, Value per part; Symbol $\sigma$, Meaning cycle-to-cycle noise of the signal, Value per part; Symbol $\lambda$, Meaning EWMA smoothing factor, Value 0.02; Symbol $s$, Meaning soft limit: share of the margin used before a warning, Value 0.5; Symbol $W$, Meaning trend window, uses, Value 400; Symbol $m_{\text{rul}}$, Meaning trend warning horizon, Value 3 shifts
A shift is 8 h. The machine's age on the dashboard is in shifts; a part's state is in uses, $n = A \cdot m$ for a machine age of $A$ shifts.

Each part is watched through one signal the PLC already has: a step time (a cylinder's reed-to-reed travel, the vacuum build-up, the belt's transit), a motor current, the compressor's duty cycle, or the colour sensor's margin. It is divided by its healthy baseline $\bar b$: $$r_n = \frac{y_n}{\bar b}$$ so $r = 1$ is as new and $r > 1$ is worse. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:68.

A part wears along a power law in its uses: $$r(n) = 1 + (r_f - 1)\left(\frac{n}{L}\right)^{p}$$ $p = 1$ is linear wear (abrasion), $p > 1$ accelerates (fatigue, a seal hardening), and a large $p$ (the gearbox's $p = 10$) is sudden onset. The part fails at $r(n) = r_f$, that is at $n = L$. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:175.

For a step time, the part fails when its tightest step reaches the PLC's watchdog $W_k$ on that step (the line then stops with an alarm): $$r_f = \min_k \frac{W_k}{b_k}$$ For the spindle it is the electronic breaker's trip (1.5 x the nominal current); for the air supply, a compressor duty of 1 (healthy duty 0.094); for the colour sensor, $r_f = 2$: the first flavour's reading crossing into its neighbour's band. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:72.

What the PLC reads is the wear times a random spread: $$y_n = r(n)\,(1 + \varepsilon_n), \qquad \varepsilon_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), \qquad \sigma^2 = \sigma_p^2 + \frac{(\Delta / \bar b)^2}{12}$$ $\sigma_p = 0.02$ is the assumed 2 % cycle-to-cycle spread of a physical step, and the second term is the PLC scan's quantisation (scan time $\Delta$: a uniform error of one scan has variance $\Delta^2/12$). Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:75, stf-cad/hbw/health.py:177.

One reading is too noisy to act on. The exponentially weighted moving average moves a step $\lambda$ towards each new reading: $$z_n = z_{n-1} + \lambda\,(y_n - z_{n-1}), \qquad z_0 = y_0$$ On a healthy machine its spread is $$\sigma_z = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2 - \lambda}}$$ which for $\lambda = 0.02$ is a tenth of $\sigma$; the price is a lag: a ramp is followed $(1 - \lambda)/\lambda = 49$ uses late. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:178, stf-cad/hbw/healththeory.py:46.

The share of the margin to failure that is left: $$\mathrm{HI}_n = 100 \cdot \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{r_f - z_n}{r_f - 1},\ 0,\ 1\right)$$ 100 = as new, 0 = failing now. A part that has failed shows 0. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:190.

Warn when the share $s = 0.5$ of the margin is used (half of it): $$z_n \ge 1 + s\,(r_f - 1)$$ For the belt: $z_n \ge 1 + 0.5 \times (1.535 - 1) = 1.267$. ($s$ is a share of the margin, not the EWMA's lag of 49 uses.) Solving the wear law for it and adding the EWMA's lag gives where it fires: $$n_s \approx L\, s^{1/p} + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}$$ The simulation agrees with this closed form within 1 % for every part (checked by healththeory.py). Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:170, stf-cad/hbw/healththeory.py:47.

The slope of the smoothed signal over the last $W$ uses, extrapolated to the failure limit: $$\hat\beta_n = \frac{z_n - z_{n-W}}{W}, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{RUL}}_n = \frac{r_f - z_n}{\hat\beta_n}$$ over the window $W = 400$ uses, and warn when fewer than 3 shifts of uses are left: $\widehat{\mathrm{RUL}}_n < 3\,m$. This catches sudden onset (large $p$) before the soft limit does. Source: stf-cad/hbw/health.py:183, stf-cad/hbw/health.py:184.

A healthy machine must never warn. Its distance to each warning, in standard deviations: $$\frac{s\,(r_f - 1)}{\sigma_z} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\beta^*}{\sigma_\beta}, \quad \beta^* = \frac{r_f - 1}{3m}, \quad \sigma_\beta = \frac{\sqrt 2\,\sigma_z}{W}$$ The model requires at least 6 for both, and runs 60,000 healthy uses per part to confirm no warning comes. Source: stf-cad/hbw/healththeory.py:50.

Two triggers renew a wear part, whichever comes first: - Predictive: its warning (soft limit or trend) fires. - Preventive interval: $0.7\,L$ uses, $\frac{0.7\,L}{m}$ shifts (stf-cad/hbw/health.py:213). Failures with no gradual precursor (a reed switch that breaks, a dirty light barrier, a broken encoder cable) cannot be predicted: a PM visit every 40 shifts tests and cleans them (stf-cad/hbw/lifecycle.py:203).

path: A part at a machine age
passages.text: The dashboard (Health, Maintenance) and the copilot's machinehealth tool place each part at the machine age $A$ the same way. With preventive maintenance on, the part is renewed each time its warning comes, so after $k$ renewals it is $n'$ uses into its current life: $$n = A\,m, \qquad k = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{n_{\text{warn}}} \right\rfloor, \qquad n' = n - k\,n_{\text{warn}}$$ With it off, $k = 0$ and $n' = n$. Then $$\text{status} = \begin{cases} \text{failed} & n' \ge T_f \\ \text{service due} & n' \ge n_{\text{warn}} \\ \text{healthy} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{warns in} = \frac{n_{\text{warn}} - n'}{m}, \qquad \text{fails in} = \max\!\left(0, \frac{T_f - n'}{m}\right)$$ and the health index is read from the part's simulated curve at $n'$. Source: web/src/shared/health.ts:15, services/api/tools.py:107.

path: Worked example: the HBW belt at 140 shifts
passages.text: The belt runs 18 uses per order, so $m = 18 \times 67.0 \approx 1{,}206.1$ uses per shift. Its law: $p = 2$, $L = 60{,}000$, $r_f = 1.535$, and the simulation warns at $n_{\text{warn}} = 42{,}401$ (by the soft limit; the closed form gives $L\,s^{1/p} + 49 = 42{,}475$). $$n = 140 \times 1206.1 = 168{,}854, \qquad k = \left\lfloor \frac{168{,}854}{42{,}401} \right\rfloor = 3, \qquad n' = 41{,}651$$ $$\text{warns in} = \frac{42{,}401 - 41{,}651}{1206.1} = 0.6\ \text{shifts}, \qquad \mathrm{HI} = 51.7$$ So with preventive maintenance on, the belt has been renewed 3 times and its next warning is 0.6 shifts away: this is the dashboard's "Next: HBW belt warns in 0.6 shifts". With it off, the same belt is 168,854 uses old, past its life of 60,000: failed.

The Maintenance page plans the next 90 shifts. For a healthy part the first service is due at the earlier of its preventive interval and its remaining life, then every interval after it: $$t_{\text{due}} = \max\!\left(0,\ \min\!\left(\frac{0.7\,L - n'}{m},\ \text{fails in}\right)\right), \qquad t_j = t_{\text{due}} + j\,\frac{0.7\,L}{m}$$ A part that is warned or failed is due now ($t_{\text{due}} = 0$). Source: web/src/dashboard/Maintenance.tsx:31. For the belt at 140 shifts: $\frac{0.7\,L - n'}{m} = \frac{42,000 - 41,651}{1206.1} = 0.29$ shifts, then every 34.8 shifts.

Wear parts used per year at two shifts a day, 250 days: $$\text{per year} = \frac{m \cdot 500}{L}, \qquad \text{stock} = \max\!\left(1,\ \left\lceil \frac{2\cdot\text{per year}}{52} \right\rceil + 1\right)$$ (two weeks of use, plus one). For the belt: $\frac{1206.1 \times 500}{60{,}000} = 10.05$ per year, stock 2. Source: stf-cad/hbw/lifecycle.py:189.

path: Copilot: how a question is answered
passages.text: The copilot answers questions about the twin in plain words, with every figure checked and every source named. This chapter describes what happens between the question and the answer: how the server decides where an answer comes from (the twin's data, its documents, the web, or a piece of research), which model writes it, what the operator sees while it works, and what is kept afterwards. Figure: An answer to "the complete math behind preventive maintenance": the route and the model's thinking folded above the derivation, every equation rendered.

The route: decided by the server, not the model
passages.text: Before any model is asked, the server decides which kind of answer the question needs (services/api/orchestrate.py, decide()). The decision is made by rules anyone can read, and the answer carries it: the route chip on the answer, and the reasons under How this answer was made. A model never decides on its own to spend a web search.

The route: decided by the server, not the model
passages.text: The signals are weighed in this order: 1. The operator's choice. Auto, Docs, Web or Deep, under the conversation. Docs never searches the web; Web and Deep always do. 2. A greeting needs no retrieval. 3. An explicit request: "deep research", "survey" or "compare sources" is research; "search the web", "latest", "news", a recent year or a price is the web. 4. The twin's own data. If the rules router called a tool that computes the twin's figures, the answer starts from them. When the question asks how such a figure is computed and the documents match, the documents come first and the twin's figures are the worked example. 5. The documents' match. The best passage's BM25 score and the share of the question's words it holds. A score of at least 6 with half the words, or 12 on

passages.text: its own, means the documents cover the question. 6. Outside knowledge. A standard (ISO 13849, IEC 62443), a vendor or "in general", with no very strong match (score 12 and three quarters of the words), goes to the web. A question about this twin (its parts, pages, alarm codes, PLC) never does: no web page knows it. Why the order. The twin's own data and documents come first because only they are true of this twin; the web is used for what they cannot hold. A web search costs about 30,000 tokens, fifteen times a documents answer, so it is spent only when the documents cannot answer. Research costs several searches, so it runs only when asked for. Without a search provider, a web question is answered from the documents and the answer says so.

passages.text: One fallback chain, the same locally and in production (chat.ORDER): 1. Gemini: the pool of Gemini models, each with its own daily quota. 2. Groq: openai/gpt-oss-120b first, which returns its reasoning; then qwen/qwen3.8-27b and openai/gpt-oss-20b. Each has its own per-minute limit, so one at its limit hands over to the next. If all are limited and Groq asks for a wait of 12 s or less, the server waits once. 3. UPB AI: the university's AI chat (UPBAIKEY, a fixed credit), the last hosted model. 4. Local: a model on this machine through Ollama (not on Render). 5. The twin's tools: when none can answer. For a question about how something works, they quote the documents' passages, equations included, rather than a one-line status. The tab above the conversation puts its provider first; the rest follow in this order. Availability

passages.text: The answer streams (POST /chat/stream, server-sent events): the route and its reasons first, then each step as it happens (the documents searched, the tools called, the model asked, a model at its limit, a search run), then the model's own reasoning, then the answer. The panel is open while the copilot works and folds above the answer when it arrives; it stays with the answer in the history. Where the reasoning comes from: - gpt-oss on Groq: its reasoning field. - qwen3 or a local thinking model: its <think block. - Gemini: the thought summaries (includeThoughts). A model that returns no reasoning shows only the route and the steps.

passages.text: Web search uses Groq's built-in browser search (services/api/websearch.py): the gpt-oss model searches, opens and reads pages on Groq's side, and the API returns every page it read. The model is told to link every claim to its page, prefer primary sources, and keep anything about the twin to the twin's own documents. - Sources are graded by their host: - trusted: standards bodies, public agencies, publishers of peer-reviewed work, manufacturers' documentation, encyclopaedias; - unvetted: anything else, shown so the operator can judge it. - Deep research splits the question into up to three web searches, runs each, and the chosen model writes the findings up with the documents' passages. - Without Groq, Gemini's built-in Google Search does the search, with its grounding sources. What is kept, and for whom
passages.text: Every visitor is a guest of their own, identified by a signed cookie. A guest's conversations and inspection photos are theirs alone. The database is Supabase Postgres when it is configured (SQLite otherwise); make db-check runs a round trip through it. Each answer is kept with its conversation, together with: - the route and its reasons; - the steps; - the model's thinking; - the sources; - the time it took. The facts it established are kept as the conversation's context; the next model is given them as Markdown.

Until Upgrade 19 the oven waited a fixed time and every cookie came out right. A real bake is heat and water: the elements heat the chamber, every door opening cools it, the cookie's surface dries and browns while its centre is still heating, and how a cookie turns out depends on the oven's state when it went in, on the dough, and on when the bake is ended. This chapter is the model of that process, built from the oven's own parts and the order's real door openings, and what it says about quality, capacity and energy. Everything is simulated; every material value is assumed and listed below, and two constants are calibrated so a nominal cookie bakes as cookies of its size do. Replace them with one measured bake before trusting the numbers.

- With a real bake the oven is the cell's bottleneck by far: the 12-cookie order takes 98 min instead of 7.1 min, 5.5 cookies an hour instead of 76.1. The rest of the cell could feed 14 ovens like this one. - A fixed timer leaves 20.4 % of cookies wrong, most of them underbaked dough from the fridge (73.9 % right). Ending the bake on the PLC's model of the cookie gets 88.9 %; correcting its colour target from the camera after every cookie gets 97.1 %: the camera sees a lot's colour after its first cookie, but not the water left in a thick cookie's centre. Measuring each piece of dough before it goes in - its temperature (an infrared thermometer) and its height (a laser distance sensor) over the presented tray - gets 99.1 %: the

hardware this upgrade asks for. - Each cookie costs about 51 Wh of heat; the oven holds 180 C on 266 W and preheats in 4.9 min (87 Wh). Two shifts a day come to about 138 kWh a month, 3.0 times the rest of the cell's 46 kWh. - The cell's microgrid was sized for a 5 W lamp: its 600 W inverter cannot run the 1300 W of elements. The oven needs its own 230 V supply, or the microgrid resizing. - After every door opening the air overshoots to at most 199 C, 51 K below the over-temperature cutout.

Three thermal nodes - the grill element ($T_t$), the bottom elements ($T_b$), the liner and walls ($T_w$) - the tray ($T_p$), and the chamber air ($T_a$), which holds 9 J/K and settles in under a second, so it is solved as a balance at every step. From ovenmodel.py: a 7.8 l chamber, an 800 W grill hairpin and two 250 W bottom hairpins, a 1.5 mm stainless liner over 10 mm of ceramic fibre, a K-type thermocouple, a convection fan, the door and the steam vent. $$C_t \frac{dT_t}{dt} = u\,P_t - \varepsilon\sigma A_t\left(T_t^4 - T_w^4\right) - h A_t (T_t - T_a) - \dot Q_{t\to c}$$ $$C_w \frac{dT_w}{dt} = \dot Q_{rad} - h A_w (T_w - T_a) - UA_{ins} (T_w - T_\infty)$$ $$\sum_k h A_k (T_k - T_a) = \left(G_{door} + G_{vent}\right)(T_a - T_\infty)$$

Quantity | Value: Quantity Element capacities $C_t$, $C_b$, Value 56.7 J/K, 101.2 J/K; Quantity Liner and walls $C_w$, Value 1412 J/K; Quantity Insulation $UA_{ins}$, Value 0.925 W/K; Quantity Shut door, steam vent at 180 C, Value 0.137 W/K, 0.616 W/K; Quantity Open mouth at 180 C (buoyant exchange), Value 3.28 W/K; Quantity The cookie's view of the grill element $F$, Value 0.079

With the door open the convection fan stops and the mouth exchanges air both ways, driven by the temperature difference (doorway flow): $$\dot V = \frac{C_d}{3}\, W \sqrt{g H^3 \frac{T_a - T_\infty}{\bar T}}$$ A PI controller on the thermocouple (first-order lag, $\tau = 10$ s) drives the solid-state relay Q9. While the door is open its integral holds and the heat is capped at 40%; even so the elements, hot from the open-door minutes, push the air to at most 199 C once the door shuts, against the 250 C cutout. Source: stf-cad/hbw/bake.py:249.

Heat-up from 21 C | : Heat-up from 21 C To 180 C, 296 s (ovenmodel.py: about 6 min); Heat-up from 21 C Elements' peak, 731 C (sheath limit 800 C); Heat-up from 21 C Air overshoot, 180.2 C; Heat-up from 21 C Holding 180 C, 266 W; Heat-up from 21 C Preheat energy, 87 Wh

A 14.6 g disc of dough, 45 mm across and 8 mm thick, in 16 layers through its thickness. The top takes radiation from the grill element and the liner and convection from the air; the bottom sits on the tray: $$\rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(k(X)\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}\right) - \rho_d \lambda \frac{\partial X}{\partial t}$$ Each layer gives up its water at a rate that follows water's vapour pressure (Clausius-Clapeyron, the same 40 kJ/mol as boiling), faster near the surface where the vapour can leave: $$\frac{dX_i}{dt} = -k_d\, \frac{p_{sat}(T_i)}{p_{sat}(100\,^\circ\mathrm{C})}\, e^{-z_i/\delta}\,(X_i - X_e)$$ Each kilogram takes its latent heat with it, so the centre holds near 100 C while the dough is wet (18-94 C in the nominal bake) - the plateau a probe in real dough shows. The evaporation is solved implicitly in each layer: it cools the

layer, which slows it. Once the surface is below 10 % water it browns (Maillard), first order with an Arrhenius rate: $$\frac{dB}{dt} = k_B\, e^{-\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_s} - \frac{1}{T_{ref}}\right)} (1 - B)$$ Source: stf-cad/hbw/bake.py:219, stf-cad/hbw/bake.py:336. Quality. A cookie is done when its centre has reached 95 C and it holds at most 6 % water (wet basis); its colour is right when the browning index lies between 0.35 and 0.65. Not done, or too pale: underbaked; too dark: burnt - the classes the camera (Upgrade 15) reports. The nominal cookie is done at 520 s and reaches the colour target 0.5 at 596 s.

%; the explicit steps are stable (Fourier number ≤ 0.5), and an unstable step is refused before it runs. - Physics: thicker or colder dough bakes longer, a hotter oven shorter, and weaker elements heat up more slowly. passages.text: Everything the cookie touches lies on one flow line: 1. The robot lays the raw cookie on the extended tray (Ofenschieber); light barrier I9 sees it. 2. The door opens, the tray retracts into the chamber (stop I6), the door closes. 3. Bake: the heating elements run (output Q9) until the cookie is done. 4. The door opens, the tray extends (stop I7). 5. The oven's own suction gripper (Sauger) lifts the cookie onto the turntable (Drehtisch). 6. The turntable stops under the saw, then turns to the belt; the pusher (Auswerfer, Q14) pushes the cookie onto the outlet belt. 7. The belt carries it through I3 onto the sorting line. One pneumatic stroke of the gripper (Q12) serves both the tray and the turntable, because the tray top, the turntable top and the belt top are all at the

passages.text: The original ft model only signals baking with a lamp. The twin's oven is built to bake: - Chamber: about 7.5 litres. Brushed stainless casing over 10 mm ceramic-fibre insulation, a 1.5 mm stainless liner inside, a stainless floor, a black enamelled top. - Heating: tubular heating elements (8 mm stainless sheath, 230 V). A grill hairpin of 2 x 400 W hangs on stainless hangers 70 mm above the cookie, in sight through the door window, and two 250 W hairpins sit on steatite standoffs under the tray, either side of its rail. Their cold ends pass through the back wall into a terminal box. - Convection fan on the back wall (motor outside the hot zone) for even heat over the tray. - Temperature sensor: a K-type thermocouple (3 mm sheath) reaches 30 mm into the chamber at

Its reading is shown on the panel's display and in Telemetry (chamber temperature, and an oven at temperature light from 170 C). - Nothing heat-sensitive inside: the tray's "in" reference I6 is not a plastic mini switch but a high-temperature inductive proximity sensor (M18, rated 230 C) mounted from below through the insulated floor. Its body and cable stay in the cool pedestal; only its ceramic face shows, 7 mm under the stainless tray when the tray is in. All other sensors and every cable are outside the chamber. - Door: a stainless frame round a triple-glazed borosilicate window. - Control panel on the oven's side: PID temperature controller with display, the solid-state relay that Q9 switches, a 10 A fuse,

Axes with this running gear: crane travel (rod and screw), crane lift (four mast tubes and screw), fork (screw), robot plunge (four columns and screw), robot reach (two rails and screw). The hardware is found from the geometry: wherever a rod, a screw or a profile runs through a part that moves relative to it along that guide, that part rides on it. It is drawn at the carriage faces and stands at most 4.5 mm proud of them. Wear: the crane's travel spindle and nut is a monitored wear part (actuator current and move time grow as the nut wears or the grease dries). Re-greasing is part of preventive maintenance.

- The belt (Q1) runs one way. There is no position feedback: I1 is a pulse switch, so the controller counts pulses from the inlet barrier (I2) to know which ejector to fire. - The colour sensor (A4, ft 128599) is not an RGB sensor: an LED shines and a phototransistor measures how much light comes back, as 0-2 V (scaled by the adapter board to the 0-10 V terminal). The reading depends on the distance and on ambient light, so the flavours are chosen to be far apart in brightness: chocolate ~340 mV, strawberry ~950 mV, vanilla ~1660 mV. - I3 after the sensor; then three pneumatic ejectors: Q3 first (weiss, vanilla), Q4 second (rot, strawberry), Q5 third (blau, chocolate). Each bay has its own light barrier (I5/I6/I7). - A bay holds up to 4 cookies; a full bay

The Verified line: the commissioned order time against the model (429.8 s vs 425.7 s, +1 %, within tolerance), faults handled, accuracy within tolerance. OEE for one shift in which every fault happens once: 30.8 % = availability 63.1 % x performance 48.8 % x quality 100 %. Low on purpose: the shift injects all seven faults. commanded pose checked), where the geometry comes from, and why the three flavours (the sensor measures brightness).

Pick a flavour (chocolate, strawberry, vanilla) and a quantity of 1 to 12, then Place order. "N raw available" says how many moulds still hold raw dough: an order can only use raw cookies, and the button is disabled when none are left. Orders queue; the cell works through them in order. Deliver N baked cookies and refill with dough appears once cookies are baked: it takes the baked cookies out and refills their moulds with fresh dough, so new orders can run. It waits until the cell is idle.
The cookie being made ("Strawberry cookie 2 of 4"), a progress bar in its flavour colour, the current step in plain words and the time left for this cookie. Running or Idle.

The camera in the sorting line's colour hood photographs every cookie; the inspection's CNN decides, and the sorting line acts on the decision. A cookie that passes is ejected to its Lagerstelle as before. A cookie that does not pass - or that the CNN is unsure of ("to a person") - is not ejected: the belt carries it to the end of the line, where it is held for the operator; its mould goes home empty, and the order makes that cookie again from the next raw dough. Next cookie gives the next cookie a fault for the inspection to catch: burnt, underbaked or cracked (good, by default). The card counts the cookies passed and rejected, and lists the last decisions: what the cookie really was, what the CNN saw and how sure it was, the autoencoder's score, and

whether the call was right, a catch, an escape (a fault passed) or a false reject. The method and the measured results are in the Vision QC chapter (docs/vision/README.md). Figure: The quality inspection card: the fault for the next cookie, and the last decision.
Every order placed this session, with its progress ("3 of 5 completed").

The 12 slots (A1-C4) and what each holds: raw dough, a baked flavour, or empty while its mould is out in the line. The summary line counts them ("11 raw · 1 in the oven line"). A slot whose cookie the inspection rejected keeps its mould but no cookie ("empty (rejected)") until Deliver refills the rack with dough; every other cookie is accounted for, so the moulds always number 12.

The actual PLC program, IEC 61131-3 Structured Text compiled by MatIEC to WebAssembly, scanned in the browser against a plant model (software in the loop). Controls: pause/run, speed 1x/4x/16x/64x, restart. The tag shows the phase (Homing, Running the order, Order complete) and the clock. - Proven line: how many of the program's decisions match the proven orchestration model (every job start is replayed in control.py), how many planted mutants the check caught, and the order time. - Units: one row per unit (crane, belt, arm, door, sauger, turntable, ovenbelt, line) with its state number and what the state means. 100 = ready, 910 = fault, 1000+ = busy in a job. - I/O image: every input and output per module, lit when on. - Jobs: the last job starts and ends, and the plant's last events. - About this program

(folded): what the run exposed, the source size, compiler and hash. Source opens the Structured Text. The plant sees only the program's outputs; light barriers, the vacuum switch, RFID and the colour sensor report what is physically there.

The operator screen, replaying the PLC's planned run of the 12-cookie order at 20x. - Units with state lights, the job each is doing and the step. - Order: how many cookies are baked and sorted, and how many returned to the rack. - Folded: Alarms (preview any alarm: cause, reaction, recovery, watchdog), Cookie trace (click a cookie: every RFID read and timestamp, and its colour reading against its record), Manual jog (which outputs each axis uses and when jogging is allowed: mode MANUAL, guard closed, hold-to-run) and Dispatch policies compared.
The rule that decides which mould moves next, each explored over every possible completion order:

Policy | What it does | Order time: Policy prefetch, What it does the crane fetches the next mould as soon as the belt is free, Order time deadlocks; Policy single, What it does one mould on the belt at a time, Order time 492.2 s; Policy reuse (used), What it does an empty mould at the hand-over is refilled with a cookie going into the rack, Order time 425.7 s; Policy buffer, What it does reuse, plus the robot parks raw cookies in a buffer while the oven is busy, Order time 425.7 s
Each module has its own I/O node (Modbus TCP) beside its controller board, so only an Ethernet line and a fused 24 V feed run to the cabinet instead of 34-way bundles.
Each module has its own I/O node (Modbus TCP) beside its controller board, so only an Ethernet line and a fused 24 V feed run to the cabinet instead of 34-way bundles.

A bar per node and signal type (DI digital in, DO digital out, AI analogue in, CNT counter/encoder, IOL IO-Link), filled by the share of channels used. Every signal of the wiring plan is on exactly one channel, with at least 20 % of each type spare. Amber means a type is fuller than that.

Node | Where | Slices: Node warehouse, Where its own plate, Slices 2 x DI8, 2 x DO8, 3 counters, IO-Link 4 (the RFID heads); Node robot, Where on the table, off every plate, Slices DI8, 2 x DO8, 4 counters; Node oven, Where its own plate, Slices 3 x DI8, 3 x DO8; Node sorting, Where its own plate, Slices DI8, DO8, AI2 (the colour sensor)

The moving cables ride in drag chains: crane travel, crane lift, robot plunge, robot reach. Each row: fill (cable cross-section in the chain, at most the rule's limit) and whether the bend radius is at least the cables' minimum (the chains use R 20 or R 12 against 10.5 mm). Hover for the devices, conductors, length and stroke.

DIN-rail use (253.7 of 355 mm, 28.5 % free; at least 20 % is required). The PLC, Ethernet switch and 4-channel electronic breaker; PE on its own busbar, power and signal in separate ducts. Folded: what changed against the original wiring, the chain rules, and the five proofs that gate the export.
Two sub-tabs. While OT security is open, the 3D view shows the network zones instead of the hazard zones.
Two sub-tabs. While OT security is open, the 3D view shows the network zones instead of the hazard zones.
7 hazards, each with its required performance level (PLr, a-e; d is the highest here):

Id | Hazard | PLr: Id H1, Hazard warehouse stacker crane, PLr d; Id H2, Hazard robot swivel arm, PLr d; Id H3, Hazard oven tray and door, PLr b; Id H4, Hazard oven turntable, saw and gripper, PLr c; Id H5, Hazard oven pusher, PLr b; Id H6, Hazard sorting ejectors, PLr b; Id H7, Hazard stored air, PLr b
Hover a row for what the hazard is and its S/F/P rating. 4 safety functions:

Id | Function | Category | PL | Devices: Id SF1, Function Emergency stop, Category 3, PL d, Devices ES1-ES3 - safety relay K0 - contactors K1/K2 + valve Y1; stop category 0; Id SF2, Function Guard interlock with locking, Category 3, PL d, Devices door switches SA-SC - K0 - K1/K2 + Y1; doors locked until standstill (ISO 14119); Id SF3, Function Safe exhaust, Category 3, PL b, Devices K0 - Y1 (monitored): air supply cut, cylinders vented; Id SF4, Function Monitored reset, Category 2, PL c, Devices S3 - K0: no restart without a deliberate reset

Proven ticks: reach (every hazard zone at least 20 mm inside the guard), fit (no guard part touches a module), logic (every combination of safety inputs checked: motion only with all E-stops released, all doors closed and locked and a reset; any single-channel fault blocks it; a door unlocks only at standstill), air (every cylinder fed only through the safe exhaust valve). Why guard locking, not a light curtain: it removes the need for a measured stopping time. The PL achieved still needs the devices' MTTFd, DCavg and CCF from their datasheets.

Zones Z0-Z5: Z0 hardwired safety (no network), Z1 cell control (the PLC and the four I/O nodes, SL 2), Z2 supervisory, Z3 energy, Z4 DMZ, Z5 enterprise and internet (untrusted). Conduits between zones carry only what is on the allow-list (25 rules for 70 program accesses). Three writable signals the program never uses are flagged. Replay an attack: pick one and compare the outcome with no protection, detection only, and the protected design. Example: a rogue coil write is blocked at conduit C1 because the source is not the PLC (port lock and static ARP). Full page opens the dashboard's security page.
Live readings of the twin, sampled 8 times a second.
Live readings of the twin, sampled 8 times a second.

Lights at the top: on (lit) or off. The warehouse light barriers (I2, I3), the robot's vacuum switch (vacuum above 50 %), oven heating (the elements are on), oven at temperature (the chamber is at 170 C or more) and the sorting line's vacuum.

Card | Readings: Card Crane, Readings travel, lift, fork (Ausleger) and belt position, in mm; Card Robot arm, Readings swivel (degrees), reach and plunge (mm), vacuum (%), what it is carrying; Card Oven & sorting, Readings chamber temperature from the thermocouple (amber above 240 C), whether the elements are heating, oven tray (slider), door and oven gripper (Sauger) position, turntable angle, bake progress (%), position along the belt path
The tag next to the title is the current cycle: the slot the mould comes from and goes to, and how far the cycle is.

Folded by default. When the live API runs, its own simulation of the original 3 x 3 machine: every joint with its tracking error (red above 1 mm), the motors' current, health and phase, and three manual commands (Retrieve B2, Store B2, Home crane). Without the API the section is absent.

One cookie's journey, as the 3D view plays it and the PLC runs it: One cookie's journey, as the 3D view plays it and the PLC runs it: 1. Retrieve: the crane travels to the mould's slot, lifts, extends the fork, takes the mould and puts it on the belt. 2. Belt and RFID: the belt carries it past RP1 and RP2; the tag is checked against the record. 3. To the oven: the robot picks the cookie off the mould and lays it on the oven tray. 4. Bake in the heated chamber. 5. Turntable, saw, pusher: the oven's gripper moves it to the turntable, which dwells under the saw and turns to the belt; the pusher puts it on the outlet belt. 6. Sort: the sorting line reads its colour and ejects it into its bay. 7. Back

to the rack: the robot collects it from the bay and puts it in a mould at the warehouse belt; the crane stores the mould. The cell overlaps cookies: while one bakes, the crane fetches the next. The PLC's dispatch policy decides what moves next; the one used (reuse) refills an empty mould at the hand-over with a cookie going into the rack. Its full 12-cookie order takes about 425.7 s in the model and 429.8 s when commissioned against the twin. Safety: every transfer takes all its locks at once and in one fixed order, and never starts unless its destination has room, so the cell cannot deadlock. This is proven over every possible completion order.

The machine fills the window. The controls float over it: - Top bar: the view switcher (searchable, Cmd/Ctrl+K), the connection status, New order, the link to the dashboard and the light/dark theme. - Dock on the left: one icon per side panel (Orders, Telemetry, PLC, Safety & security, Remote I/O, Connectivity, Commissioning, Geometry, Analysis). - Panel: opens next to the dock. Unpinned it floats over the 3D view as frosted glass; pinned it takes its own column and the view moves aside. Drag the grip on its edge to resize it (300-640 px); click the grip to fold the panel away. - Control bar at the bottom: the run state and current step, Place an order when the cell is idle, and the view toggles.

Toggle | What it does: Toggle Enclosure, What it does Shows or hides the guard: frame, polycarbonate panels, doors, and the E-stops, door switches and their cables mounted on it. Hide it to watch the machine.; Toggle Hazard zones, What it does Shows the swept envelope of each moving machine, coloured by its required performance level (PLr).; Toggle Wiring, What it does Opens the legend of cable colours: 24 V, 0 V, PE, mains, digital in/out, encoder, analogue, air, safety, bus, IO-Link.
Opening Safety & security OT security replaces the hazard zones with the network zones: blue boxes for cell control (the I/O nodes and the PLC), red for the hardwired E-stops and reset.

Key | Action: Key 1-9, Action Open panel 1-9 (in dock order); Key [, Action Show or hide the panel; Key P, Action Pin or unpin the panel; Key C, Action Show or hide the enclosure; Key Cmd/Ctrl+K, Action Search and switch views; Key Esc, Action Close the floating panel or the view switcher
Shortcuts are ignored while typing in a field.

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan. Labels in the scene: the rack's state above the warehouse ("Rack: raw dough only", or how many are baked), and in OT security view the name and IP address of each I/O node, the PLC cabinet, the E-stops and the reset button.

Every axis is driven by one shared timeline. While an order runs: the crane fetches a mould, the belt carries it to the robot, the robot moves the cookie into the oven, the elements glow and the chamber heats, the oven's own gripper moves it to the turntable, the saw and the pusher work it onto the outlet belt, the sorting line reads its colour and ejects it into its bay, and the robot brings it back to the warehouse. Light barriers flash red while a cookie cuts their beam.

A digital twin of a fischertechnik Smart Tabletop Factory (536634, 24 V) that bakes cookies. One parameter table per module drives the 3D view, the FreeCAD models, the drawings and every analysis, so the CAD, the kinematics and the I/O can never drift apart.

A digital twin of a fischertechnik Smart Tabletop Factory (536634, 24 V) that bakes cookies. One parameter table per module drives the 3D view, the FreeCAD models, the drawings and every analysis, so the CAD, the kinematics and the I/O can never drift apart. Every placement is checked by proofs before it is exported: no two parts intersect in any allowed pose, every part is carried by something, and the workpiece clears every station on its whole journey. Everything is simulated. There is no physical machine connected; the "Live" or "Simulation" chip in the top bar says whether the physics API is running or the twin runs entirely in the browser.

- Warehouse (high-bay warehouse, ft 536631): a 3 x 4 rack (slots A1-C4) and a stacker crane with travel, lift and a telescopic fork (Ausleger); a belt carries moulds to the robot. - Gripper robot (vacuum gripper robot, VGR, ft 536632): a cylindrical robot (swivel, plunge, reach) with a suction cup. It links every station. - Oven (multi-processing station with kiln, ft 536632): tray (Ofenschieber), heated chamber, its own suction gripper, turntable with saw, pusher and an outlet belt. - Sorting line (ft 536633): belt, colour sensor, three pneumatic ejectors and three bays (weiss, rot, blau). Around them: a guard enclosure with doors and E-stops, a PLC cabinet, four remote I/O nodes, a central air station, an edge computer (OPC UA, MQTT Sparkplug, Unified Namespace), drag chains and the wiring.
Exactly 12 cookies exist in the system, each in its own mould. Three flavours, chosen so the colour sensor (which measures reflected brightness, not colour) can tell them apart:
Flavour | Sensor reading | Bay: Flavour chocolate, Sensor reading ~340 mV, Bay blau; Flavour strawberry, Sensor reading ~950 mV, Bay rot; Flavour vanilla, Sensor reading ~1660 mV, Bay weiss
Raw dough is pale. A cookie gets its flavour colour when it is baked.
